questions.question: Is the reported Spearman computed per group and averaged, weighted by group size or pair count, or pooled across all observations?
questions.rationale: Pooling mixes within-group order with cross-group score offsets, which a translation-invariant ranking loss never pins down ([Yan et al. 2022](https://research.google/pubs/scale-calibration-of-deep-ranking-models/)). A per-group average gives a two-item group, which carries one bit, the same weight as a 25-item group with 300 pairs (inference).
questions.interpretation: **Pooled:** part of both numbers measures the cross-group calibration of a head that was never trained for it. Evaluate the BCE logit or an anchored score instead. **Per-group average:** the value is driven by groups of two or three, so compare it with a pair-weighted concordance before reading anything into the plateau.
questions.answer: The required selection metric eval_macro_spearman is the unweighted mean of eligible, defined per-assay Spearman correlations. eval_spearman aliases the observation-count-weighted mean; neither pools scores across observations and neither weights by pair count. Historical illustrative 0.41/0.20 numbers in the spec are not assumed to be matched macro results.

questions.question: Which groups enter the metric? How are size-one groups, constant groups and ties created by median aggregation handled? Does the eligible fraction differ between splits?
questions.rationale: Spearman is undefined for constant groups. The median of an even number of replicates can create exact ties. An eligibility rule that differs from the training rule scores pairs the loss ignored.
questions.interpretation: If the eligible fraction or tie rate differs between the two test partitions, part of the gap is compositional rather than a failure to generalize.
questions.answer: The actual headline requires n>=3 and pChEMBL span>=0.5, excludes constant labels, and uses average ranks for exact ties. Size-one and size-two assays are excluded. Constant predictions produce undefined rho, excluded with defined coverage recorded. A test has 8278/16431 eligible assays (50.38%); B has 3972/9578 (41.47%). Headline labels are float32 tensor values promoted to Python float. The raw exported float64 B test labels instead admit 3971 assays; correcting that precision reproduces the native test macro exactly (0.1768796098004701) on identical saved scores.

questions.question: Do the two test partitions differ in group-size distribution, within-group score variance, near-tie rate or replicate count?
questions.rationale: Each of these bounds the attainable per-group correlation, independently of the model (inference).
questions.interpretation: If Split B's groups are smaller, flatter or noisier, reweighting Split A's per-group results to Split B's mix should reproduce part of the drop without any retraining.
questions.answer: Yes. A/B test assay-size medians are 3/2, but means are 11.73/14.30; mean within-assay variance is 0.30457/0.18086; exact tied-pair fractions are 6.20%/5.65%; replicated-row fractions are 3.22%/3.91%. Training-RMS near-tie fractions are 60.80%/61.89%. These describe composition, not a causal share of the split gap; model-score reweighting remains pending.

questions.question: How large is the spread over seeds, over a bootstrap of indivisible split units, and over alternative Split B realizations?
questions.rationale: Split realizations built to identical criteria differed in difficulty while preserving method rankings ([Petti & Eddy 2022](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC8929697/fullTextXML)). A sparse learning-rate grid produced a standard deviation 6–7 times the seed-to-seed value ([Xin et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11379)).
questions.interpretation: A realization spread near the 0.21 gap means the gap itself is poorly estimated. Comparisons within one realization, such as model against baseline, stay trustworthy either way.
questions.answer: Whole-unit intervals are available for the initial B checkpoint and completed cheap baselines, conditional on one fitted seed and allocation. Original splitter seeds 42/43/44 yield identical assignments. Seeded equal-size tie ordering produces two additional dependent validation/test reallocations with unchanged training support; 86592/94118 held-out rows move. Per-allocation validation checkpoint/LR selection and multi-seed performance spread remain pending. These allocations do not measure training-support or split-geometry variation.
questions.native_A_prefix_update: A epochs 1-4 have whole-assay intervals, conditional on one fitted trajectory; this does not add independent seeds or split realizations.

questions.question: Does the metric tolerate small score differences the way the loss does? How do top-weighted metrics move?
questions.rationale: The loss deliberately declines to order near-ties and emphasizes the top of each group. Spearman weights every pair equally.
questions.interpretation: A large difference between Spearman and a tie-aware or epsilon-band concordance means the metric and the loss disagree about what counts as an error. If top-k metrics keep improving after Spearman plateaus, the loss is optimizing something the metric does not reward.
questions.answer: Spearman has no explicit noise band beyond exact ties, unlike the ranking margin. On the fixed B selected test predictions, ordering accuracy is 0.5892 with no band, 0.6305 outside log10(3), and 0.6581 outside the training replicate-RMS band; these use different denominators, not improved predictions. On the same 3969 eligible validation assays, NDCG@1/@3 peak at epoch11, whereas NDCG@5 and macro Spearman peak at epoch6. By epoch15 all three NDCGs are below their epoch6 values (changes -0.00589/-0.00116/-0.00431). The later top-ranking maximum is descriptive, not significant evidence of objective conflict. All-nonconstant-group NDCG instead peaks at epoch8 for top1/3, so mismatched cohort definitions can alter the conclusion. Matched A and controlled comparisons remain pending.
questions.native_A_prefix_update: A epochs 1-4 native snapshots have noise-band and group-size metrics. On the same 7997 eligible validation assays NDCG@1/@3/@5 rises from 0.59835/0.66331/0.71098 at epoch 1 to 0.65891/0.70869/0.74848 at epoch 4. Full-horizon peaks remain unknown.

questions.question: Which term of the composite validation loss rises first on each split: BCE, the ranking loss, or each direction of the contrastive loss? Does BCE AUC move with BCE log-loss?
questions.rationale: The aggregate is dominated by whichever term has the largest magnitude times weight. Each term can rise for reasons unrelated to ranking.
questions.interpretation: If BCE log-loss rises while AUC and Spearman stay flat, that is the calibration pattern and it does not harm ranking. If the ranking term's own loss rises, the model is overfitting the target. If logits grow uniformly, log-loss rises sooner on the split where discrimination is weaker, which alone could produce a turning point at 10% on one split and 30% on the other (inference).
questions.answer: In the fresh B run, BCE validation loss reaches its minimum at epoch2 (0.44531), ranking loss at epoch5 (2.79392), and contrastive/aggregate loss at epoch15 (5.83497/6.68790). By epoch15 BCE is 0.48300 and ranking loss 2.92871, while AUROC improves from 0.73865 at epoch2 to 0.77202. Thus auxiliary classification discrimination can improve while its log-loss worsens, and decreasing dominant contrastive loss hides worsening ranking loss. Contrastive direction and fixed-scale trajectories are available; matched A remains pending. First adjacent increases occur at BCE2->3, ranking3->4 and contrastive/total6->7; these local fluctuations are not statistical change points.
questions.native_A_prefix_update: A epochs 1-4 native validation BCE decreases 0.52074->0.48617->0.46223->0.46034, ranking loss 2.66708->2.61290->2.57423->2.54027, and contrastive loss 4.86771->3.32545->2.72154->2.42469. AUROC rises 0.72635->0.77144->0.79702->0.80344. These are an observed prefix, not final turning points; directional contrastive inference remains pending.

questions.question: Are checkpoints selected on aggregate loss or on validation Spearman? Where do the best-loss and best-Spearman checkpoints fall on each split?
questions.rationale: Selection is part of the method.
questions.interpretation: If the best-Spearman checkpoint comes much later than the best-loss checkpoint on Split B, the early turning point is a selection artifact, not the model's limit.
questions.answer: The fresh B run selects on validation macro Spearman: epoch6, 0.18460015. Minimum aggregate validation loss occurs at epoch15 (6.68790), whose macro Spearman is lower, 0.17561471. These rules therefore choose different checkpoints. In this run the macro optimum is earlier, not later, than the loss optimum. Matched A and multi-seed selection-rule comparisons remain pending.
questions.native_A_prefix_update: A validation-only calibration through epoch 4 gives T=1.11777 and log-loss 0.46034->0.45857 at epoch 4. This is in-sample validation fitting, not selected-test transfer or a completed trajectory.

questions.question: How do training and validation ranking metrics diverge over time on each split?
questions.rationale: This separates fitting non-transferable features from a limit on signal or capacity.
questions.interpretation: Training Spearman rising while Split B stays flat from early on suggests fitting specific to training units. Both flat suggests little learnable signal.
questions.answer: For the fixed 2048-assay B training probe, eligible macro Spearman rises from 0.18336 at epoch1 to 0.53189 at epoch15. Validation rises from 0.11006 to its peak 0.18460 at epoch6, then ends at 0.17561. The widening gap supports training-specific fitting in this run, with later training improvements transferring poorly. This is a descriptive training probe and one seed, not a full-training metric or a completed matched A/B comparison.
questions.native_A_prefix_update: A fixed eligible training-probe macro rises 0.16214->0.22805->0.27084->0.30188 at epochs 1-4; validation rises 0.16488->0.21244->0.24317->0.26145. Full-horizon behavior remains unknown. The original B uniform-assay probe and current eligible-assay probe are not identical sampling designs.

questions.question: Does the early rise survive with frozen encoders?
questions.rationale: Full fine-tuning with randomly initialized heads distorts pretrained features ([Kumar et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.10054)).
questions.interpretation: If the rise disappears or comes later with frozen encoders, encoder drift drives it. If it persists, the interaction module or the heads drive it.

questions.question: Does the learned contrastive temperature keep sharpening? Does the contrastive validation loss still rise against a fixed candidate pool?
questions.rationale: InfoNCE values depend on the number and similarity of in-batch candidates ([van den Oord et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.03748)) and on temperature ([Wang & Liu 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.09740)).
questions.interpretation: A rise that vanishes under a fixed pool or a fixed temperature is an artifact of batch composition or overconfidence. A rise that persists alongside a widening gap in positive-pair alignment between training and validation indicates memorization.
questions.answer: The learned logit scale rises 13.5999 -> 18.4685 -> 22.5461 at epochs1/6/15. Each split uses one unchanged candidate-pool hash across epochs, and baseline validation already fixes its candidate pool. B validation contrastive loss declines 8.54974 -> 6.00606 -> 5.83497; rescoring identical representations at scale13 gives 8.52970 -> 5.82207 -> 5.55379. Sharpening increases validation loss relative to fixed-scale rescoring, but the fresh run has no sustained aggregate contrastive-loss rise. Fixed-temperature retraining and matched A remain pending; rescoring alone does not establish a training benefit.
questions.native_A_prefix_update: A native scale rises 13.5412->14.5521->15.5213->16.4275 at epochs 1-4 while aggregate validation contrastive loss falls. Directional/fixed-temperature A inference is implemented but awaits the completed protected trajectory and free authorized GPUs.

questions.question: Is the rise concentrated in particular group sizes or similarity strata?
questions.rationale: This localizes where fitting fails to transfer.
questions.interpretation: Concentration in low-similarity groups supports fitting that is specific to the training distribution. A uniform spread supports calibration drift.
questions.answer: Scalar localization is complete for initial B epochs1-15 and A epochs1-4. B row-weighted BCE rises from epoch2 to15 in every assay-size bin (overall +0.03768). The macro-Spearman decline from epoch6 to15 is -0.00899; three-item assays contribute 76.1% of that net change, with their macro dropping 0.08247. Overall paired component interval [-0.02078,0.00302] includes zero; the three-item interval [-0.15882,-0.00549] is conditional on one fitted trajectory, observed endpoints and unadjusted multiple strata. B has no shared-scaffold groups under the binary relation. A BCE declines in shared/mixed/unseen groups across epochs1-4, but later behavior, native listwise/contrastive loss localization and repeated comparisons remain pending.

questions.question: Which split matches deployment? Will future y mostly be near neighbours of known y, or come from new regions?
questions.rationale: Park and Marcotte accept random splits only when the warm regime is the sole regime of interest. DataSAIL's authors say leakage-reduced splitting is the wrong choice when application data resemble training data ([DataSAIL](https://github.com/kalininalab/DataSAIL)).
questions.interpretation: **Warm deployment:** 0.41 is the relevant number and Split B is a stress test. **Cold deployment:** Split B is the target, and Split A should not drive tuning.
questions.answer: Deployment is unseen generated molecules, as specified by the user. Unseen identity does not imply unseen scaffold. Report the unseen-molecule cell of Split A and the unseen-scaffold stress test in Split B; the future mixture cannot be inferred without generator outputs.
questions.evidence: User deployment clarification; tier1/data/overlap_A_test.parquet and overlap_B_test.parquet

questions.question: How is each test y's maximum similarity to training y distributed in both splits, and how does Split A perform in each similarity stratum?
questions.rationale: One recent similarity-aware evaluation found only **16 of 873** random-split test samples below one-third similarity, with performance falling sharply among them ([Zhang et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.09481v1)).
questions.interpretation: If Split A's lowest stratum scores near 0.20, Split B measures a stratum that Split A barely contains, and there is no anomaly to explain. If that stratum stays near 0.41, something other than similarity drives the drop.
questions.answer: Binary scaffold support is fully measured on both held-out partitions. In A test, 19.29% of rows and 21.33% of unique molecules have unseen scaffolds; B is entirely unseen. Fixed depth-3 A test Spearman is 0.1342 on shared-scaffold rows within assays and 0.0669 on unseen-scaffold rows after reapplying eligibility; B is 0.0607. Complete all-unseen A assays instead score 0.1067 (233 eligible assays), showing the cohort distinction matters. Matched neural strata and seed/realization comparisons remain pending.
questions.native_A_prefix_update: At A epoch 4, complete shared/mixed/unseen-scaffold validation assays score 0.27008/0.24807/0.18514; unseen-scaffold rows within assays score 0.19547 on a different cohort. Composition standardization changes common-support validation macro 0.26158->0.25561. Full-horizon, selected-test and repeated comparisons remain pending.

questions.question: What is the size distribution of indivisible units in each partition? Were units assigned at random, or did large units default to training?
questions.rationale: Single-linkage grouping lets a few "bridge" members merge otherwise dissimilar groups, and larger families fail to split more often ([Petti & Eddy 2022](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC8929697/fullTextXML)).
questions.interpretation: A giant training unit alongside small, peripheral test units means Split B's test set was selected for remoteness. Non-random assignment also breaks the exchangeability between validation and test units that checkpoint selection relies on.
questions.answer: A uses 131450/16431/16431 whole-assay units in train/val/test, median size 3 in all, maxima 49020/1409/1147. It randomly reserves one anchor assay per target-sequence then randomly allocates remaining assays. B has 570/4032/4034 scaffold-assay components, median sizes 6/5/5, maxima 1661628/7382/5683. Its giant and 569 target-coverage rescue units are forced into training; the rest are balanced by rows and positive rate into val/test. The giant supplies 98.70% of B training rows. This is not exchangeable random assignment across train and held-out units and does not by itself quantify a causal performance penalty.
questions.evidence: tier1/supervision_composition_v2/complete.json and *_units.parquet; original split manifests; reward_model/training/random_assay.py and scaffold_component_split.py

questions.question: Do the positive rate, score distribution or group descriptors differ across partitions, and does a formal test flag the difference?
questions.rationale: Label shift alone can move Spearman without any change in inputs. BBSE tests for label shift using any black-box classifier whose confusion matrix is invertible ([Lipton et al. 2018](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/lipton18a.html)). Classifier two-sample tests show where two samples differ ([Lopez-Paz & Oquab 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.06545)).
questions.interpretation: A significant shift in labels or group descriptors assigns part of the gap to composition. It also argues for re-splitting with class-ratio constraints, as DataSAIL does.
questions.answer: Yes. B partition-local positive rates are 0.67904/0.79295/0.79024 in train/val/test. Whole-unit descriptor C2ST balanced accuracy is 0.8522/0.8594 for B train-val/train-test, versus 0.5170/0.5181 for A; all four Holm-adjusted permutation p-values are 0.003. Val-test tests are near chance (A0.4958/B0.4966; adjusted p=1). These classifiers use raw-source descriptor labels and a fixed logistic model; unit assignment constraints limit population/exchangeability interpretation. B BBSE estimates test positive prior 0.78498 (unit interval0.66963-0.87895), versus actual0.79024 used only diagnostically; its class-conditional invariance assumption is unverified. A BBSE awaits matched model predictions.

questions.question: Which x appear in Split B's test groups, and how many training groups does each have?
questions.rationale: x is assumed to be warm, but thin coverage of x turns part of Split B into the harder neither-seen setting.
questions.interpretation: If test x have few training groups, part of the gap comes from coldness on the x side. Report Split B separately by each x's training count.
questions.answer: All 1723 B test proteins occur in training, with 1-1303 distinct training assays per protein (median24 across proteins; median127 when weighted by test-assay frequency). At the original macro-selected B checkpoint, test macro Spearman by training-assay count is 0.0539 for1, 0.0849 for2-5, 0.1829 for6-20, 0.1626 for21-100 and 0.1935 for>100; eligible assay counts are71/149/311/1184/2257, all defined. Whole-component intervals are [-0.0701,0.1748], [0.0018,0.1716], [0.1324,0.2345], [0.1350,0.1891], [0.1710,0.2148]. Low-support estimates are weak/uncertain and bins differ in composition; this is not a causal coverage effect. Complete target identities and counts are saved in test_targets.parquet.

questions.question: Across model variants, do Split A and Split B scores move together?
questions.rationale: Out-of-distribution accuracy often tracks in-distribution accuracy linearly ([Miller et al. 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.04649)). The relation is "largely dataset-dependent" ([Wenzel et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.09239)) and sometimes inverse ([Teney et al. 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.00613)).
questions.interpretation: A tight line means tuning on Split A is a valid proxy. A flat or inverse relation means tuning on Split A actively misleads. All of this evidence is classification accuracy on images, so applying it to grouped rank metrics is an extrapolation.

questions.question: What is the replicate-based noise ceiling of the chosen metric on each split?
questions.rationale: A noise ceiling marks the point where "any remaining mismatch is then attributable to the noise in the measurements" ([Nili et al. 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3990488)). The replicates that are currently aggregated by median make it computable: split each pair's replicates into halves, score one half against the other with the headline metric, and apply a Spearman–Brown correction.
questions.interpretation: If Split B's ceiling is lower, part of the gap is a difference in measurement quality, and the right report is the fraction of the ceiling reached. Two caveats apply. Spearman–Brown assumes parallel measurements ([SAGE](https://sk.sagepub.com/ency/edvol/embed/the-sage-encyclopedia-of-research-design-2e/chpt/spearman-brown-prophecy-formula)), and this research found no ML precedent for a noise ceiling on a grouped rank metric.
questions.answer: Test split-half macro Spearman is A 0.5445 versus B 0.3780; the requested Spearman-Brown heuristic is A 0.7050 versus B 0.5485. Coverage is only 420/8278 (5.07%) and 348/3972 (8.76%) eligible assays, respectively. These conditional heuristics do not establish a ceiling or fraction-of-ceiling result for the entire test set.

questions.question: How does within-group variance of s divide among the y-cluster main effect, the x×y interaction, and replicate noise?
questions.rationale: Generalizability theory estimates exactly this interaction component, and it needs replication to separate the interaction from residual noise ([G-theory notes](https://marklhc.quarto.pub/psyc520-2025spring/slides/07-g-theory.html)). Cross-attention can only add value on the interaction share (inference).
questions.interpretation: A small interaction share means Split A's 0.41 rested largely on y main effects that do not transfer across similarity regions. In that case 0.20 sits near the cold-y limit for any architecture (hypothesis). Because most y are seen about twice, fit the model at the y-cluster level.
questions.answer: The requested raw-measurement variance model and an assay-balanced sensitivity fit are complete, but the decomposition is unstable. A test within-assay interaction contribution changes from 0 to 0.1159204 pChEMBL squared; B changes from 0.1716375 to 0.0567531. Training noise estimates conflict with direct replicate disagreement. A stable interaction share or architectural ceiling is not established; raw noise is not median-label uncertainty.

questions.question: What fraction of within-group pairs differ by less than the replicate noise?
questions.rationale: Near-ties add noise to both training and evaluation.
questions.interpretation: A large fraction lowers the ceiling and argues for tie-tolerant losses and metrics.
questions.answer: Training-only raw-replicate RMS differences are A 0.78055 and B 0.76605 pChEMBL. The test pair fractions with label gaps at or below those bands are A 60.802% and B 61.887%. Under the same original margin log10(3), fractions are A 42.297% and B 43.640%. These bands describe raw-replicate disagreement, not uncertainty intervals for aggregated medians.

questions.question: Why do only half the groups support ranking supervision, and does that half differ in size, variance or x?
questions.rationale: The ranking head learns from a subset that may not represent the evaluation groups.
questions.interpretation: A systematic difference means the ranking head is trained on a different distribution from the one it is evaluated on, even on Split A.
questions.answer: The actual float64-cache sampler admits 63867/131450 A and 72202/145454 B training assays (48.59%/49.64%). Most exclusions are n<3 (62516/67994); another 5067/5258 have insufficient span. Headline evaluation uses float32 labels and admits 63867/72201: two A assay memberships differ but cancel in the count, and one B membership differs at the span boundary. Under headline precision, eligible versus ineligible training assays have median size 11 versus 1, mean variance 0.5360 versus 0.0863 on A and 0.5492 versus 0.0918 on B. Target-frequency total variation is 0.2904/0.2908; 3420/3393 of 7873 training targets have no headline-eligible assay. These are systematic composition differences. Evaluation uses the same nominal n>=3/span>=0.5 rule, with the small precision discrepancy documented separately; most excluded assays are also excluded from the headline metric.

questions.question: How were pairs chosen for observation, given the 70% positive rate?
questions.rationale: If pairs were observed because they looked promising, unobserved pairs are unlabeled, not negative.
questions.interpretation: If observation was selected by promise, in-batch "negatives" are partly positive. That changes how contrastive negatives and baselines should be built.
questions.answer: The recorded curation retains exact numeric pChEMBL measurements on both sides of the activity threshold from single-protein binding assays with confidence score >=8 and no recorded variant; parent/structure/quality checks and within-assay medians follow. The activity-balanced resplit changes assignment, not source-row inclusion. Original curated positives are 69.04%; numeric archived measurements in the retained assays are already 69.2176% positive. Provenance differs sharply: literature 67.79%, BindingDB patents 82.86%, PubChem 4.61%. Original experimental sampling frames, pair inclusion probabilities and tested-but-unpublished results cannot be recovered from these tables. Preferential testing of promising pairs is unproven; missing observations remain unlabeled, and these proportions do not estimate activity prevalence among generated molecules.
questions.evidence: tier1/observation_process/{complete.json,verification.json}; source/output hashes and independent raw SQL counts verified. The 2126775 records lacking numeric pChEMBL include 1345088 kinetic endpoint records and are not distinct unobserved pairs or negatives.

questions.question: How many groups have all members on one side of the threshold, and how far is the threshold from the replicate noise?
questions.rationale: BCE carries no within-group ordering information for items on the same side of the threshold.
questions.interpretation: If many groups are all-positive, BCE contributes little to the ranked target and mostly shapes calibration and x priors.
questions.answer: With current partition-local binary labels, A all-positive/all-negative assay counts are train 63190/28715, val 8069/3537, test 7791/3524; B counts are train 69799/30457, val 4683/2443, test 4919/2664. Same-side labels occur in 43.63%/54.20% of ranking-eligible A/B test assays, so BCE has no within-assay label-order preference there. At threshold6, 35.58%/32.21% of test rows have pair medians within the training raw-replicate RMS band 0.78055/0.76605. This proximity is not median-label uncertainty or proof that BCE cannot help shared features; loss-subset performance remains pending.

questions.question: Are batches built from whole groups or from observations, and is the fraction of ranking-eligible groups per batch fixed?
questions.rationale: The ranking loss is defined on only about half the groups, so its effective weight fluctuates with batch composition.
questions.interpretation: Large fluctuation means adaptive loss-weighting methods read noise. Use stratified batches before comparing objectives.
questions.answer: Batches contain bounded assay lists plus classification-only rows, not independent pair rows or every member of every large assay. In the exact configured epoch-zero ordering, the ranking-eligible list fraction averages 0.5583 on A and 0.5625 on B, with standard deviations 0.1468/0.1474; the 5th-95th percentiles are 1/3 to 5/6 on both. Each split has one local batch with no eligible ranking list. Eligibility is not stratified to a fixed fraction. Counts cover all 12,820/14,020 local microbatches; they reconstruct the sampler, not historical device traces.

questions.question: Does the contrastive loss treat other positives of the same x in the batch as negatives?
questions.rationale: With group batching and diagonal-only targets, a positive anchor in a 25-item group at 70% positives sees about 16–17 labeled positives as negatives (inference). Standard two-tower practice masks only identical candidate IDs ([TFRS](https://www.tensorflow.org/recommenders/api_docs/python/tfrs/tasks/Retrieval)).
questions.interpretation: If co-positives are treated as negatives, the contrastive loss directly opposes the BCE and ranking losses. Masking them, or using multi-positive targets, is the first fix to test.
questions.answer: The reference already hides own-assay co-candidates and masks cross-assay same-protein and duplicate-query-molecule entries. Those observed same-protein negatives are zero in the audit. Global training-known positives can remain negatives when sampled under another protein. Across 512 deterministic epoch-zero batches per split, these are 0.530%/0.714% of protein-to-molecule negative comparisons on A/B (0.437/0.576 per active anchor), and 0.441%/0.657% in the reverse direction. A gradient fixture verifies their negative push. This is a lower bound from any curated training observation above 6, not all biological positives, and does not establish the performance impact of masking them.
questions.evidence: reward_model/model/losses.py; tests/test_paired_generalization_sampling_audit.py; tier1/sampling/{A,B}/complete.json and known_false_negative_batches.parquet on Atum

questions.question: Are the contrastive projections taken before or after cross-attention?
questions.rationale: Pair-independent embeddings allow cheap in-batch negatives and a full softmax over all 8,000 x. Pair-dependent embeddings require recomputing cross-attention for every off-diagonal pair.
questions.interpretation: This architectural detail determines which contrastive remedies are feasible.
questions.answer: Before cross-attention. In the reference mlp_contrastive mode, separate protein and molecule projections consume pooled encoder outputs and produce normalized, pair-independent embeddings. Ranking and BCE consume fused representations. Cross-pair contrastive scores therefore require embedding products, not new cross-attention passes.

questions.question: How is the listwise loss normalized across groups of different sizes?
questions.rationale: Summing over pairs lets the roughly 10% of large groups dominate the gradient. Per-group averaging matches a per-group-averaged metric (inference).
questions.interpretation: If loss weighting and metric weighting differ, the model is optimizing groups the metric barely counts.
questions.answer: The reference sums top-weighted Plackett-Luce selections within each sampled list, with tie-averaged weights 1/(sqrt(list size)*log(position+1)), then averages sampled lists. It does not divide by the retained selection-weight sum. Larger original assays receive ceil(n/32) bounded ranking-list opportunities, so this is not equal weighting of original assays. The controlled comparison separately implements within-list normalization and inverse-opportunity assay balancing without changing sampled rows or update counts.

questions.question: Are x frequencies in batches skewed, and is any sampling-probability correction applied?
questions.rationale: Uncorrected in-batch softmax is biased under power-law frequencies ([Yi et al. 2019](https://research.google/pubs/sampling-bias-corrected-neural-modeling-for-large-corpus-item-recommendations/)). The y-to-x direction can learn an offset for x popularity (inference).
questions.interpretation: A strong x-popularity component in the contrastive branch is a shortcut that needs no information about y.
questions.answer: Yes: across the configured first epoch, the top 1% of 7,873 proteins supply 30.07% of A and 30.64% of B assay-list opportunities. The median is two lists per protein, versus maxima 1,587/1,589. The reference has no sampling-probability/log-Q correction. This establishes skewed candidate frequency, not that the learned contrastive score actually uses a popularity shortcut; that requires pathway/probe evidence.

questions.question: Are subsets for ablations and learning curves drawn by indivisible unit?
questions.rationale: Subsampling by observation leaks similar items back into training.
questions.interpretation: Only subsampling by unit gives interpretable learning curves on Split B.
questions.answer: E41 uses nested whole assays on A and whole scaffold-assay components on B, with subset-local binary labels. Eight views and actual 10% A/B production loading/sampler checks are complete. questions.question: What ranking quality does each loss deliver alone, and in each pair, on each split?
questions.rationale: A loss-subset grid measures each loss's contribution and their interactions directly. Arms without the ranking head are scored by the BCE logit or the contrastive similarity.
questions.interpretation: An interaction term that is positive on Split A and negative on Split B means the auxiliary losses help in-distribution but hurt transfer (hypothesis).

questions.question: How well do the ranking head, the BCE logit and the contrastive similarity agree within groups, and does their agreement fall during training?
questions.rationale: This quantifies the stated mismatch between ranking order and contrastive geometry.
questions.interpretation: Near-zero within-group correlation between contrastive similarity and s means the contrastive branch encodes cross-group compatibility, not within-group order.
questions.completed_scope: All 15 B validation/training-probe epochs plus selected test. Validation ranking-BCE agreement falls 0.6798 to 0.6017 while ranking-cosine rises 0.0743 to 0.2341. This is not general scorer divergence or proof of gradient conflict. Matched A trajectory remains pending. Trainer-float32-label rescoring is complete and preserves these validation agreement values; all 93 export/scorer native-metric parity comparisons passed.
questions.native_A_prefix_update: A epoch 1->4 validation ranking-BCE agreement rises 0.63066->0.66557 on 7995 mutually defined eligible assays; paired assay interval for change [0.02468,0.04435]. Ranking-cosine rises 0.12360->0.28508 on 7997, change interval [0.14908,0.17335]. This does not establish full-training behavior or gradient alignment.

questions.question: How much of the BCE head's validation AUC does an x-only model reproduce?
questions.rationale: Within-group Spearman ignores anything constant within a group, but BCE rewards per-x base rates (inference).
questions.interpretation: If an x-only model recovers most of the AUC, BCE mostly teaches x priors that do not affect within-group order.
questions.answer: Protein-only frozen-feature BCE validation AUROC is 0.6687445 on A and 0.6452095 on B. The identity/scaffold lookup degenerates to protein priors on B and achieves validation AUROC 0.6914818 with constant within-assay scores. The matched deep-model A comparison remains pending; AUC ratios do not causally attribute model signal.
questions.native_A_prefix_update: A epoch 4 neural validation AUROC is 0.80344; the completed protein-only baseline is 0.66874. This early checkpoint comparison cannot replace validation-selected final-model results or causally attribute an AUC fraction.

questions.question: Do the auxiliary gradients align with the ranking gradient in the encoders and in cross-attention?
questions.rationale: Gradient conflict flags interference in optimization, but low conflict does not predict good generalization ([Royer et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08910); [Mueller et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.14677)).
questions.interpretation: Frequent conflict points to a problem. Its absence rules nothing out.

questions.question: Were the loss weights tuned, and on which split's validation data?
questions.rationale: Weights tuned on random-group validation optimize for the warm regime.
questions.interpretation: If the weights change when tuned on Split-B-style validation data, the value of the auxiliary losses depends on the shift.
